# Modeling count data: Poisson and negative binomial {#sec-count-regression}













[The introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) left a promise on the table. It showed you the PDGFR-β counts (@fig-glm_counts_by_dpi), pointed at the floor and the fan, and said that a Gaussian model would fail on them, without letting you watch it happen. This chapter keeps that promise first. Then it goes on to two things the introduction set aside: the fact that every animal's section has a different area (the fix, an *offset*, comes later in this chapter), and the zeros that spike counts, unlike these, are known for. The PDGFR-β counts never drop below about ninety cells, which is a luxury. Spike counts, and most counts you'll collect in an electrophysiology rig, are not so kind.

I'll say something about how the chapter is put together, because it changes scene halfway. We start on the histology counts you know. We fit the Gaussian model the last part would have reached for, watch what it does, and swap the family until the model fits what a count is: first a Poisson, then a negative binomial. Then we read the one number the negative binomial adds, `shape`. Then we give those counts what they've been missing, a denominator. And then we leave the microscope for the rig, where a new kind of zero appears and the negative binomial, on its own, can't explain it.

## First attempt: pretend it's Gaussian

Two things about how I'm treating the histology counts for now, so you can hold me to them. First, there is one row per animal (49 animals, 49 rows), so there is no nesting to worry about here. Second, I'm going to ignore something I know. The sections do not all have the same area: `Tissue_Area`, the area of the section over which the cells were counted, runs from about 6 to 20 mm², and it shrinks as the days go by. A raw count therefore mixes "more cells" with "more tissue counted". For now, the count is the count. And because we want the whole time course, including the sham animals at day 0, I'll treat `DPI` as a categorical predictor, exactly as in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, so each day gets its own mean and I don't have to assume a straight line through a curve I already know isn't straight.

I could tell you why a Gaussian is a bad idea for counts, and you'd nod. I'd rather show you, because seeing a model fail on your own data teaches more than being warned about it. So here is the straight linear model, one mean per day and one common `sigma`, fit with the flat `brms` defaults, the same deliberate choice @sec-linear-regression-multiple made, so the data speak with as little interference as possible, and beside its `lm` counterpart.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_gauss <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit8.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

The `Intercept` is the day-0 mean (about 513 cells) and each `DPI_f` coefficient is how far that day sits from it, just like the categorical predictor in @sec-linear-regression-multiple. Sampling is healthy, and the means themselves are perfectly reasonable summaries. The trouble is `sigma`: a single number, around 700, meant to describe how far an animal typically sits from its day's mean.

The coefficients aren't wrong. What a model *believes* about the world lives in the data it would simulate, and that's what @sec-mcmc-model-checking taught us to check. So let's ask the model to generate fake animals, day by day, and see whether they look like real counts. I'm using `posterior_predict()` to draw new observations (not just new means) and `ggdist`'s graded intervals to show where the model thinks a new animal would land, with the real animals on top and a dashed line at zero.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pp_gauss <- posterior_predict(fit_gauss, ndraws = 1000)

pp_long <- data.frame(
  y = as.vector(pp_gauss),
  DPI_f = rep(cell_data$DPI_f, each = nrow(pp_gauss))
)

ggplot(pp_long, aes(x = DPI_f, y = y)) +
  stat_interval(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  geom_point(data = cell_data, aes(y = Pdgfrb_Pos),
             color = "black", size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Predictive\ninterval") +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β+ cells per section") +
  Plot_theme
```

![Where the Gaussian model expects a new animal's count to fall on each day (bands are 50%, 80% and 95% predictive intervals), against the observed animals](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-count_gauss_predictive-1.png){#fig-count_gauss_predictive width=624}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
neg_share <- tapply(colMeans(pp_gauss < 0), cell_data$DPI_f, mean)
```
:::






On days 0 and 3 the bands spill below zero: the model thinks there is a 24% chance that a new day-0 animal has a *negative* number of cells, and about 27% for day 3. Nobody has ever counted minus three hundred pericytes. And notice the second problem, which you've met before: the bands are exactly as wide on day 3 as on day 7, because there is only one `sigma`. The real animals disagree. The standard deviation of the counts runs from about 190 cells on day 0 to over 900 on day 7. This is the same complaint @sec-linear-regression-multiple ended on, a single `sigma` that's too generous for the tight groups and too stingy for the loose ones, only now the tight groups are pushed against a wall.

One quieter thing before we move on: the *means* stayed sensible. The Gaussian's failure is in what it thinks is possible around them, in the predictions and the uncertainty, which is exactly where it would hurt you if you reported an interval for a new animal, or trusted the standard errors on the low-count days.

## Same question, new clothes: Poisson with a log link

The smallest change that respects what a count *is* is to swap the family for the Poisson, the distribution for counts of independent events at a steady rate, and the link for the log. That's it: same formula, same predictor, two changes. In `brms` it's one argument. I'm using the `brms` defaults again while we learn the structure; remember the warning from the introduction about priors on the link scale, because later in this chapter I set one deliberately.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_pois <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = poisson(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit9.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::

:::

Read these coefficients carefully, because they're not on the scale you're used to. They're on the *link* scale, the log scale. The `Intercept` of about 6.24 is $\log(\mu)$ for day 0, so the expected day-0 count is $e^{6.24} \approx 513$, the same mean the Gaussian gave. The `DPI_f7` coefficient of about 1.43 isn't "1.43 more cells", it's "1.43 more on the log scale", and adding on the log scale means multiplying on the count scale: $e^{1.43} \approx 4.2$, so day 7 has about four times as many PDGFR-β+ cells as day 0. This is the price of the doorway: you can't read a coefficient off the summary and add it to a count anymore, you have to translate through the inverse link. What you gain is that the model can never predict fewer than zero cells.

The floor problem is gone. What about the fan? Let's find out whether the Poisson family's *own* idea of how variance should behave matches the data. A Poisson count has one defining property: its variance equals its mean. Here are the two side by side, one point per day, on log axes, with the variance each family says a group should have.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
day_stats <- aggregate(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data,
                       FUN = function(x) c(m = mean(x), v = var(x)))
day_stats <- do.call(data.frame, day_stats)
names(day_stats) <- c("DPI_f", "m", "v")

sigma_gauss <- summary(fit_gauss)$spec_pars["sigma", "Estimate"]
mu_grid <- exp(seq(log(350), log(4000), length.out = 100))

var_lines <- data.frame(
  mu = mu_grid,
  Poisson = mu_grid,
  Gaussian = sigma_gauss^2
)
var_lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Poisson, family = "Poisson"),
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Gaussian, family = "Gaussian")
)

line_labels <- var_lines[var_lines$mu == max(var_lines$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.3))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

vm_ratio <- day_stats$v / day_stats$m
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Variance against mean for each day's counts (points), and the variance each family assumes (lines). Both axes are logarithmic.](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-count_pois_variance-1.png){#fig-count_pois_variance width=624}
:::
:::






The Gaussian says the variance should be the same no matter the mean: that's the flat grey line, and the points refuse to lie on it. The Poisson says the variance should equal the mean: the orange diagonal. The points *do* climb with the mean, so the Poisson has the right instinct, but they sit about two orders of magnitude above the line: each day's variance is between 71 and 401 times its mean, where a Poisson says 1. The day-7 group, for instance, has a variance near 850,000 where a Poisson expects about 2,100. The standard summary is the [dispersion statistic]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, the sum of squared Pearson residuals divided by the residual degrees of freedom, which should be near 1 for a well-specified Poisson [@inchausti2023; @gelman2020].






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dispersion <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
disp_pois <- dispersion(glm_pois)
```
:::






Ours is about 236. To see what that means for the predictions, I'll do what we did for the Gaussian: ask the fitted model to generate data and compare. This time I'm using `pp_check()`, and truncating the axis at 6,000 because a few Poisson replicates wander out further than any real animal.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior predictive check for the Poisson model. The observed counts (dark line) are far more spread out than any replicate (light lines).](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-count_pois_ppcheck-1.png){#fig-count_pois_ppcheck width=576}
:::
:::






The replicates (light lines) are lumpy little spikes, one cluster for the low days and one for the high ones, because the model believes each day's counts cluster tightly around their mean. The observed density (dark line) is a single broad plateau. The Poisson family fixed the floor and got the direction of the variance right, and it is still off by a factor of hundreds, which means every interval it reports would be wildly too narrow. A GLM isn't a spell: it gives you a family, and if the family's idea of noise is wrong, the model is wrong, just in a more respectable-looking way.

## Changing one word: the negative binomial

So here is the natural question: can a count model fail and then, with a small change, work? Yes. And the change is the whole point of having a *framework* instead of a menu of separate techniques.

Why is the Poisson too tight? Think about what it assumes. It describes what you'd see if every animal in a group had the same true density of PDGFR-β+ cells and the only randomness was which cells happened to fall inside your counting window. But animals aren't identical. Some mice just have more pericytes in that patch of tissue than others, before you ever count anything. So your count is noisy twice: once because you sampled a window, and again because the *underlying rate* itself differs from animal to animal. The Poisson has room for the first kind of noise and none for the second.

The [negative binomial]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} family adds exactly that second source. It is a Poisson whose rate varies from animal to animal, and it does so with one extra parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean: $\text{Var}(y) = \mu + \mu^2/\phi$, where a larger $\phi$ means less extra scatter, and $\phi \to \infty$ gives the Poisson back [@inchausti2023]. Same linear predictor, same log link. In `brms`, the change is one word.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_nb <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit10.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

The coefficient table looks almost the same as the Poisson's: the same log-scale means, the same fourfold jump at day 7. That's the point: the *mean model* didn't change. What changed is `shape` (the $\phi$ above), which the Poisson didn't have, and which is now estimated to be around 4.9: small enough that the extra variance is substantial. Now the same check as before, side by side with the Poisson.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_pois <- pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Poisson")

p_nb <- pp_check(fit_nb, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Negative binomial")

p_pois + p_nb
```

Now the replicates are broad enough to cover the observed density instead of ignoring it. They aren't perfect: their right tail reaches past 6,000, further than any animal we counted, so the negative binomial is slightly generous with the high counts. That's a much smaller sin than being off by a factor of hundreds. And the mean-variance picture finally has a curve that runs through the points. I'm adding the negative binomial's variance function, $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$, to the same plot as before.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shape_nb <- summary(fit_nb)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"]

var_lines_nb <- rbind(
  var_lines,
  data.frame(mu = mu_grid, v = mu_grid + mu_grid^2 / shape_nb,
             family = "Negative binomial")
)
line_labels_nb <- var_lines_nb[var_lines_nb$mu == max(var_lines_nb$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.4))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40",
                                "Negative binomial" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +

  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

![The same variance-against-mean plot, now with the negative binomial's variance function](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-count_nb_variance-1.png){#fig-count_nb_variance width=624}
:::
:::






Strictly speaking, the negative binomial isn't "a Poisson that works": it's a different family. But nothing else in the model moved: the predictor, the log link, the formula, the way we read coefficients. That's what "generalized" buys you. The choice of noise is a dial you turn independently of the rest.

Since the log link now gives us trustworthy uncertainty, let's finally read the effect the way it deserves to be read: as a ratio. Each `DPI_f` coefficient exponentiates to a fold change relative to day 0. A half-eye shows the whole posterior for each ratio, not just an interval, on a log axis so that "twice as many" and "half as many" are the same distance from 1.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
draws_nb <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))
day_cols <- c("b_DPI_f3", "b_DPI_f7", "b_DPI_f14", "b_DPI_f30")

fold <- data.frame(
  day = factor(rep(c(3, 7, 14, 30), each = nrow(draws_nb)), levels = c(30, 14, 7, 3)),
  fold_change = exp(unlist(draws_nb[, day_cols]))
)

ggplot(fold, aes(x = fold_change, y = day)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2", point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Fold change in PDGFR-β+ cells vs. day 0 (log scale)",
       y = "Days post-ischemia") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior fold change in PDGFR-$\beta$+ cell count relative to day 0 (negative binomial model, raw counts). The dashed line at 1 means no change.](count-regression_files/figure-html/fig-count_fold_raw-1.png){#fig-count_fold_raw width=624}
:::
:::






Day 3 straddles the dashed line: no detectable change from the day-0 baseline. Then day 7 jumps to roughly four times baseline, day 14 to roughly six times, and day 30 comes back down a little, to about four. That's a delayed surge, which makes biological sense for cells that respond to injury after the acute phase is over, and it's a very different picture from the "no change" a low-count Gaussian's overconfident intervals would have hidden. One caution about the reference point: day 0 is the sham group, so every one of these fold changes compares an ischemic animal at some time point to a sham animal. It cannot separate the effect of the ischemia from the effect of the passage of time, because there are no sham animals at later days (the design limit we met in @sec-linear-regression-multiple).


## What `shape` is really telling us

A few pages ago I reported the `shape` of the negative binomial, said it was "small enough that the extra variance is substantial", and moved on. That was a bit like handing you a thermometer reading without saying which way is hot. So before we add anything, let me go back to that fit and read it properly.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shape_draws <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))$shape
```
:::






Here is the way I like to think about `shape`. Imagine two pericyte-rich animals on the same day after ischemia. Even before you put a section under the microscope, one of them simply has more PDGFR-β+ cells in that territory than the other, for reasons that are biological and not your fault. The negative binomial says each animal has its *own* true density, and that those densities scatter around the day's mean by a multiplicative wobble. `shape` (which I'll write $\phi$, as in the previous chapter) is the dial that controls how big that wobble is: the animal-to-animal coefficient of variation of the true rate is $1/\sqrt{\phi}$ [@inchausti2023]. A large $\phi$ means the animals are almost interchangeable; as $\phi \to \infty$ the wobble vanishes and you're left with the Poisson. A small $\phi$ means animals are individuals.

For our fit, `shape` has a posterior median of 4.8, so before we have counted a single cell, animals of the same day already differ by about 46% in their true PDGFR-β+ density. That figure answers a question that comes up at the bench all the time: *if I count more cells per animal, will the noise go away?* The total variance of a count is $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$, so its coefficient of variation, the standard deviation relative to the mean, is

$$
\text{CV}(y) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\mu} + \frac{1}{\phi}}
$$ {#eq-cv-nb}

The first term is the counting noise: it shrinks as the count grows. The second is the animal-to-animal noise: it doesn't depend on the count at all. I'll draw both against each other, with the Poisson (which has only the first term) for contrast, and the observed CV of each day's animals as points. I'm using the CV, not the variance as in the plot above, because the CV is on the scale a scientist thinks in ("the counts wobble by 40% or so"), and it turns the two noise terms into a picture: one keeps falling, the other is a floor.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

phi_sub <- shape_draws[seq(1, length(shape_draws), length.out = 400)]

cv_band <- data.frame(
  mu = mu_grid,
  lo = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) quantile(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub), 0.025)),
  mid = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) median(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub))),
  hi = sapply(mu_grid, function(m) quantile(sqrt(1 / m + 1 / phi_sub), 0.975)),

)

day_cv <- aggregate(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data,
                    FUN = function(x) c(m = mean(x), cv = sd(x) / mean(x)))
```

### Which `shape` is it? The same number under several names

`shape` in `brms` is the `theta` that `MASS::glm.nb()` prints, and in both the variance is $\mu + \mu^2/\text{shape}$; `glmmTMB`'s `nbinom2` family uses the same form. Other software parametrizes the same distribution with the *reciprocal*, $1/\phi$, so that zero means "Poisson" (a small number, then, is a good sign there, and a large number is a bad one). Whenever you read a paper that reports "the dispersion parameter", check which of the two it is before you decide whether the data are overdispersed.

## "Per what?": the offset

Every scientist has had the following conversation. You report that treated animals have 1,900 PDGFR-β+ cells and the controls have 500. Somebody at the back asks: *per what?* A count is like a receipt with the shop's name torn off: it tells you how many, and it says nothing about how big the window was that you looked through. If sections differ in size, the count mixes two things: how dense the cells are, and how much tissue you counted.

`cell_data` does have that denominator. `Tissue_Area` is the area of the section, in mm², over which the cells were counted. (There's a second column, `Tisue_Area`, with a typo in its name: it is the very same measurement in µm², a million times bigger, so I won't use it; @sec-eda-data-quality shows the check and explains the choice.) I set that aside earlier in the chapter, when I said the count was the count. It isn't.

### What an offset does

The idea is old and simple. If the counting window is $A_i$ and the true density of cells is $\theta_i$, then the expected count is the density times the window, $\mu_i = A_i \theta_i$. Take logs, and the window turns into something we can add:

$$
\log(\mu_i) = \log(A_i) + \log(\theta_i) = \log(A_i) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots
$$ {#eq-offset}

The term $\log(A_i)$ is called an **offset**. It is a predictor whose coefficient isn't estimated but fixed to exactly 1, which is how the model says "double the window, double the expected count" [@gelman2020; @inchausti2023; @mcelreath2020]. What remains on the right, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots$, is now a model for the *density*: cells per mm², not cells per section. The coefficients keep the interpretation they had before (log fold changes), but the thing being multiplied is a rate.

Before fitting I need priors on the log scale, and I'd like to keep them judged on the *outcome* scale, per the warning in [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro). With the offset, the `Intercept` is the log of the density (cells per mm²) of a day-0 animal with a typical section size. In [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) the day-0 mean was about 500 cells, over sections of about 14 mm², so around 35 cells/mm². I'll use `Normal(4, 1.5)`, which puts 95% of its mass between roughly 3 and 1,100 cells/mm², a range that comfortably includes what we saw and is far from "anything goes". For the day coefficients, `Normal(0, 1.5)` allows fold changes from about 1/20 to 20, wider than anything the biology here would deliver (the largest change we saw last time was under tenfold). I keep `brms`'s default for `shape`, an inverse-gamma(0.4, 0.3), which is weakly informative and keeps the parameter away from zero.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_hist <- c(
  prior(normal(4, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)

fit_offset <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f + offset(log(Tissue_Area)),
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_hist,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: callout-note
### An offset is an assumption, not a discovery

The offset says the expected count is *exactly proportional* to the area. Nothing in the data forced that: it comes from how the counting was done. The textbook way to check it [@gelman2020; @mcelreath2020; @inchausti2023] is to put $\log(A_i)$ in the model as an ordinary predictor with a free coefficient and see whether 1 is a believable value for it. So let me do that.
:::






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_free <- c(prior_hist, prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "log_area"))

fit_free <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f + log_area,
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_free,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

b_area <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_free))$b_log_area
```
:::






The coefficient of log-area comes out at 0.06 [-0.96, 1.01]. The interval is wide enough to contain 1 (the value the offset imposes) and also 0 (the value that would say area doesn't matter at all). The data cannot tell those apart, and the reason is worth understanding: area and day are tangled up, since the sections get smaller as the days go by, and within a single day the areas are fairly similar. There isn't enough independent variation in area to learn what it does on its own. Comparing the two models by leave-one-out cross-validation says the same thing, that neither is predicting new animals better.

## A new scene: spikes

Now to the second promise. Take the histology hat off and put on the electrophysiologist's. Suppose you record 150 single units from cortex, half from control animals and half from animals given a drug that is supposed to quiet spontaneous activity. For each unit you count the spikes emitted in a window of spontaneous activity. **Does the drug reduce firing?**

::: callout-note
### These data are simulated, on purpose

I don't have a real electrophysiology dataset with the structure I need yet, so for now I generated one, in `functions/simulate_ephys.R`, with a fixed seed. In real experiments the units come from a handful of animals, so they are not independent of each other; I treat them as independent here to keep the chapter about counts, and @sec-multilevel-glmm is where that shortcut gets repaired.

### The negative binomial, with an offset

Duration is the exposure, so the offset is $\log(\text{duration}_i)$, and the model is for the firing rate in spikes per second. Priors again on the outcome scale. The `Intercept` is the log firing rate of a control unit in Hz, and `Normal(-1.5, 1.5)` puts 95% of its mass between about 0.01 and 4.5 spikes/s, the range in which the spontaneous firing of cortical neurons plausibly lives. The group coefficient is a log rate ratio: `Normal(0, 0.7)` allows rate ratios from about 0.25 to 4, which is more than any single drug should manage. The `shape` keeps its default.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_spk <- c(
  prior(normal(-1.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.7), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
)

fit_nb_spk <- brm(
  spikes ~ group + offset(log(duration_s)),
  data = spikes,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_spk,
  init = 0,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit3.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

With `brms`'s default random starting values, this model was hit by a chain that drifted into a degenerate corner of parameter space, where the counts are "explained" by a vanishing mean and an astronomically large `shape`, and never came back. The summary showed an `Rhat` of 3 and hundreds of divergent transitions, which is the sign the chapter on MCMC taught you to respect: don't read that fit. For counts, the right check isn't the density overlay of the earlier chapters: with discrete data and a spike at zero, a kernel density smooths away the one thing we care about. A **rootogram** is designed for this [@gelman2026].     coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 40)) +
```{.r .cell-code}
    labs(title = "Rootogram", x = "Spikes in the window")
  p2 <- pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "zeros", ndraws = 500) +
    labs(title = "Share of zeros", x = "Proportion of units with 0 spikes")
  p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.4, 1))
}
```

## Two kinds of silence: zero inflation

A picture that helps me here: you ask a room of people how many times they checked their phone during your talk. Some of them answer zero because they don't own a phone. Others own one, and just happened not to check it. The two zeros mean different things, and no amount of rethinking the distribution of the *phone owners* will explain the first kind: it's a different process, a group of people for whom the count is impossible. In the rig it's the same. An active unit with a low firing rate can well emit no spikes in a short window, by chance alone; a unit that's silent under these conditions (whatever the reason: hyperpolarized by inhibition, not part of the active ensemble, damaged by the electrode) emits none however long you listen.

A **zero-inflated** model writes exactly that as a mixture. With probability $\pi_i$ a unit is silent and produces a zero; with probability $1 - \pi_i$ it's an active unit whose spike count follows the negative binomial, which has its own zeros too:

$$
P(y_i = 0) = \pi_i + (1 - \pi_i)\,\text{NB}(0 \mid \mu_i, \phi), \qquad P(y_i = k) = (1 - \pi_i)\,\text{NB}(k \mid \mu_i, \phi) \text{ for } k \geq 1
$$ {#eq-zinb}

There are now two models to write: one for the rate of the active units, $\log(\mu_i) = \log(\text{duration}_i) + \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{treated}_i$, which is what we had; and one for the probability of being silent, $\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1\,\text{treated}_i$. That's the logit doorway of @sec-logistic-regression again, now for the probability that a unit belongs to the silent state. In `brms`, the second model is a second formula for the parameter `zi`. That gives me two questions instead of one: *does the drug change how fast the active units fire, and does it change how many units are silent?* I'll use the priors from before on the rate model. For the silence model, I borrow the logic of @sec-logistic-regression: on the logit scale, `Normal(0, 1.5)` for the intercept and the coefficient spreads the prior over the whole range of probabilities. I also set the `shape` prior explicitly to the one used above, because `brms` 2.22's default for the zero-inflated family is a nearly flat gamma(0.01, 0.01), and I want the two models to differ in the structure I'm testing, not in an accidental prior.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_zi <- c(
  prior_spk,
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", dpar = "zi")
)

fit_zinb <- brm(
  bf(spikes ~ group + offset(log(duration_s)), zi ~ group),
  data = spikes,
  family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_zi,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit4.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

### Zero-inflated, or a hurdle?

There is a close cousin I owe you a mention. A **hurdle** model also has a "zero part" and a "count part", but it organizes them differently: a first stage decides whether the unit fires *at all* (crossing the hurdle), and the count of the second stage is drawn from a distribution that can't produce zeros (a zero-truncated negative binomial). In a hurdle, every zero comes from the first stage; in a zero-inflated model, zeros come from both. The choice is scientific: a hurdle is the natural model if crossing zero is a distinct qualitative event (a cell either engages or doesn't, and the interesting quantity is how strongly it engages once it does), and zero inflation is the natural one if some zeros are structural and others are just unlucky draws from an active process. Here's the hurdle version, for comparison.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
  prior_spk,
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "hu"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", dpar = "hu")
)

fit_hurdle <- brm(
  bf(spikes ~ group + offset(log(duration_s)), hu ~ group),
  data = spikes,
  family = hurdle_negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_hu,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/count-regression_fit5.rds",
```

The comparison separates the negative binomial from the two models with a zero part, by a margin of nearly four standard errors, and it can't separate the zero-inflated model from the hurdle. No observation has an unreliable Pareto-k in the zero-inflated fit. That's the honest structure of this choice: the data say "*there is a zero part*"; they don't say which of two stories about it is right. That's a decision about the biology, and it needs evidence from outside the count table, for instance whether units that are silent in this window respond in another (in which case "silent" is a state and the zero-inflated story fits) or whether they are never recorded firing at all. I'll keep the zero-inflated version, on those grounds, and I'll be specific about what its parameters mean.

::: callout-warning
### Model comparison doesn't replace the check

The comparison above says the zero-inflated model predicts new units better than the plain negative binomial. That's a *relative* statement about a set of three candidates. It's the rootogram, not the table, that tells us the winner is a credible description of the data rather than "the least bad of three".
:::

## What did the drug do?

A zero-inflated model answers with several numbers, and the honest report needs each one in the units that a colleague understands. The rate model lives on the log scale, so I exponentiate to get a rate ratio; the silence model lives on the logit scale, so I push it through the inverse logit to get probabilities. Working on the posterior draws, as in @sec-logistic-regression, means each quantity arrives with its uncertainty.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
draws_zi <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_zinb))

effects <- data.frame(
  rate_ratio = exp(draws_zi$b_grouptreated),
  p_silent_control = plogis(draws_zi$b_zi_Intercept),
  p_silent_treated = plogis(draws_zi$b_zi_Intercept + draws_zi$b_zi_grouptreated),
  rate_control = exp(draws_zi$b_Intercept)
)
effects$silent_diff <- effects$p_silent_treated - effects$p_silent_control
```
:::






The two effects, on the two parts of the model, are these. **Among active units**, the treated ones fire at 0.61 [0.47, 0.79] times the rate of the controls (a control unit that's active fires at about 0.25 [0.21, 0.29] spikes per second). **The share of silent units** is 19 [11, 28]% in the controls and 30 [20, 42]% in the treated units, a difference of 12 [-2, 25] percentage points.






::: {.cell}

The rate effect is clear: the whole posterior sits below 1. The silence effect is less so: the treated units are more likely to be silent, but the credible interval for the difference reaches below zero, so with 150 units I'd call it suggestive, not settled. That is a finding in itself: the plain negative binomial's single rate ratio (0.54 [0.36, 0.81]) is the two effects blurred into one number. What the drug did to the *average* unit, the thing a single-number summary reports, is a combination of the active units firing slower and more units falling silent, and the model with a zero part is the only one that can pull the two apart.

If you still want the single number (a manuscript will ask for one), `posterior_epred()` gives the expected count for each unit, silent ones included, and setting the recording length to one second turns it into a mean firing rate in spikes per second across the population of units.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nd_rate <- data.frame(group = factor(c("control", "treated"), levels = levels(spikes$group)),
                      duration_s = 1)
mean_rate <- posterior_epred(fit_zinb, newdata = nd_rate)
mean_rate_ratio <- mean_rate[, 2] / mean_rate[, 1]
```
:::






The population-mean firing rate is 0.20 [0.16, 0.24] spikes/s in the controls and 0.10 [0.08, 0.13] in the treated units, a ratio of 0.52 [0.38, 0.72]. That number is smaller than the rate ratio among active units, because it contains both mechanisms. Neither is "the effect of the drug"; the honest sentence describes both, and says which one you're reporting.

::: callout-note
### What I put in

Since I wrote the generator, I can check the answers. Active control units fired at 0.25 spikes/s, the drug multiplied that by 0.6, and the probability of being silent went from 20% to 35%; the true `shape` was 2. The model recovers each of them with the truth inside its interval, including the modest silence effect that 150 units can barely resolve. That's a check that the model can find what is there, not a guarantee that it would in a real dataset, where the mechanism isn't known.
:::

### Does the prior matter?

I promised in the last chapter to stop asking you to trust priors on faith, so here is the sensitivity check for this model: the same fit with a narrower and a wider prior on the two treatment coefficients (the rate and the silence).

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_narrow <- c(
  prior(normal(-1.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b", dpar = "zi")
)
prior_wide <- c(
  prior(normal(-1.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"),
  prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi"),
  prior(normal(0, 5), class = "b", dpar = "zi")
)

zi_formula <- bf(spikes ~ group + offset(log(duration_s)), zi ~ group)

fit_zinb_narrow <- brm(zi_formula, data = spikes, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
                       prior = prior_narrow, seed = 123,
                       file = "models/count-regression_fit6.rds", file_refit = "never")
```

The rate effect is nearly indifferent to my choice: the narrow prior shrinks it a little (from about -0.5 to about -0.4 on the log scale) and the conclusion, a slower firing rate, is the same under all three. The silence effect is more sensitive, as you'd expect from a parameter that rests on 150 units, of which 39 recorded no spikes at all: the narrow prior pulls it down by about a third, and under every one of the three priors the interval still includes zero. That agrees with the previous figure, and it's the reason I called the silence effect suggestive: the data lean toward "the drug silences more units" but don't settle it, and a reader with a skeptical prior would be entitled to stay unconvinced.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

`MASS::glm.nb()` and `glmmTMB` fit the same models by maximum likelihood, and for the mean parts they land close to `brms`: the offset model gives a day-14 log fold change of 2.22 in `glm.nb` and 2.12 in `brms`, and the treatment rate ratio among active units is 0.6 in `glmmTMB` against 0.61 in `brms`. The small gap in the fold change is the weakly informative prior pulling a little toward zero. This is the usual story of this book: with a weak prior and a decent sample, the likelihood does the work. The raw-count negative binomial from the start of the chapter says the same: its day-7 log-scale coefficient is 1.43 in `glm.nb` and 1.42 in `brms`.

Two differences are worth knowing. `shape` is where they drift: `glm.nb` reports `theta` = 5.3 for the histology offset model where `brms` reports a posterior median of 4.8. The posterior of a dispersion parameter with 49 animals is skewed, and a maximum-likelihood point estimate and a posterior summary are two different summaries of a skewed thing, which is also why a frequentist fit of a dispersion parameter from a few animals per group can be unstable. The second difference is more consequential: zero-inflated likelihoods can be flat or multimodal in the parameters of the zero part, especially with few silent units, and a frequentist fit may then return a silence probability at the boundary (exactly 0 or 1) or fail to converge. In our data, `glmmTMB` gives a silence coefficient of 0.7 and a Wald interval for it of [-0.09, 1.49], close to the Bayesian one; with fewer units, the weakly informative prior on the silence coefficient would be doing something practical, keeping the estimate away from the edge, and not just something philosophical.
:::

## Can we trust the sampling?

This chapter has fitted ten `brms` models, and I said "sampling is healthy" about a few of them and warned you about one chain that wandered off in another. A vague reassurance is cheap. A table isn't, so here are the same three checks as in @sec-mcmc-model-checking for every fit in the chapter: Rhat below 1.01, both effective sample sizes above 400, and no divergent transitions. ## Where this leaves us

We started with a promise and two loose ends from the introduction to this part, and they turned out to be the same kind of lesson. The promise was to watch a Gaussian fail on counts and to fix it by changing the family, which the Poisson did only halfway and the negative binomial did. The `shape` of a negative binomial is a statement about how different the *units* are from each other before you count anything, and it sets a floor on the noise that counting more cannot lower, which is a statement about your experimental design. An **offset** gives a count its denominator: it fixes the coefficient of $\log(\text{exposure})$ to 1, turns the model into one for a rate, and, in the histology data, changed the size of the time course because the tissue shrank while the cells piled up. It's an assumption of the design, and the data could not tell us whether it was right, so I used it for the reason that we counted over a known window. And when a count has more zeros than any negative binomial can honestly explain, the honest model separates two kinds of silence, the neurons that can't fire from the ones that didn't, and lets you ask two questions of a drug instead of one.

One shortcut runs through the whole chapter, and I've flagged it twice: every unit and every animal was treated as independent of the others. Real units come from a few animals, and the count of an animal's units is not the same as the number of independent pieces of evidence. @sec-multilevel-glmm is the chapter that repairs it. Before that, @sec-beta-robust-regression turns to outcomes that are continuous but bounded (proportions of time in a zone) or heavy-tailed (reaction times), the last two families of this part.
